n: In January 588 BC, Nebuchadnezzar’s whole army surrounds Jerusalem and builds siege works around it. Jews later remembered this date with a fast day.

f.w: the tenth month, in the tenth day of the month

f.g: Siege walls or towers built around a city to attack it and block escape.

n: The siege drags on for about a year and a half, into Zedekiah’s eleventh year.

f.w: the eleventh year of king Zedekiah
f.g: About 586 BC (some date it 587 BC).

n: By midsummer the food runs out completely. Lamentations describes the horror of famine during this siege.
When the Babylonians break through the wall, Zedekiah and his soldiers flee at night through a gate near the royal garden, heading east toward the Jordan Valley.

f.g: The wall was breached.
Hebrew Arabah—the Jordan Valley, toward Jericho.

n: The Babylonians catch Zedekiah near Jericho, and his army deserts him.
Zedekiah is brought to Nebuchadnezzar’s field headquarters at Riblah in Syria for sentencing as a rebel vassal who had broken his oath.

Zedekiah’s sons are killed before his eyes—the last thing he ever sees—and then he is blinded and taken to Babylon. The Book of Mormon reveals that one son, Mulek, escaped and was led to the Americas.

f.g: Ezekiel had foretold Zedekiah would be brought to Babylon yet not see it (Ezekiel 12:13).
Bronze chains or shackles.

n: About a month later, Nebuzaradan, commander of Nebuchadnezzar’s guard, arrives to finish the job.

f.g: Literally “chief of the butchers” or executioners—commander of the royal bodyguard.

f.w: the fifth month, on the seventh day

n: He burns Solomon’s temple, the palace and every important house. The temple had stood for nearly four centuries; Jews still mourn its loss each year on the ninth of Av.

f.w: burnt the house of the LORD

n: The army tears down Jerusalem’s walls, leaving the city defenseless. Nehemiah would rebuild them about 140 years later.
The rest of the population, including those who had defected to Babylon, is deported.

f.w: fell away to the king of Babylon
f.g: Deserted to Babylon’s side, as Jeremiah had urged (Jeremiah 38:2).

n: Only the poorest are left to tend vineyards and fields, so the land would not become completely wild.

f.g: Vineyard workers and farmers.

f.w: left of the poor of the land

n: The great bronze pillars, stands and the huge bronze basin Solomon made are smashed so the metal can be hauled to Babylon.

f.g: A huge bronze basin of water for priestly washing, resting on twelve bronze oxen.

n: All the smaller bronze utensils used in temple sacrifices are taken as well.

f.g: Tools for trimming lamp wicks.

n: Anything made of gold or silver is carried off too. Some of these vessels later appear in Belshazzar’s feast and were returned under Cyrus.

f.g: Pans for carrying hot coals from the altar.

f.w: such things as were of gold

n: The bronze of Solomon’s pillars, sea and stands was so great it could not be weighed—a poignant reminder of past glory now lost.

f.g: Too much to weigh.

n: The narrator pauses to describe one pillar: about 27 feet tall with a 4½-foot bronze capital decorated with chainwork and pomegranates. Lingering on the detail expresses grief over what was destroyed.

f.g: A cubit is about 18 inches (45 cm), the length from elbow to fingertip.
The capital, or decorative top, of a pillar.

n: Nebuzaradan arrests the chief priests and temple gatekeepers. Seraiah the chief priest was an ancestor of Ezra the scribe.
He also takes military officers, royal advisers, the scribe in charge of the draft, and sixty prominent men—those seen as leaders of the rebellion.

f.g: Sixty (a score is twenty).
Enrolled or called up for military service.

n: These leaders are brought to Nebuchadnezzar at Riblah.

f.w: brought them to the king of Babylon

n: They are executed, and the narrator sums up the tragedy in one line: Judah was exiled from its land. The covenant warnings of Deuteronomy have come true.

f.w: So Judah was carried away out of their land

n: Nebuchadnezzar appoints Gedaliah as governor over those left behind. Gedaliah came from Shaphan’s family, which had supported Josiah’s reforms and protected Jeremiah.

f.w: Gedaliah the son of Ahikam, the son of Shaphan

n: Surviving Judean army captains and their men gather to Gedaliah at Mizpah, his new capital north of Jerusalem.

f.g: A town a few miles north of Jerusalem, in Benjamin.

n: Gedaliah urges them to accept Babylon’s rule and settle down peacefully—the same counsel Jeremiah had given.

f.w: serve the king of Babylon; and it shall be well with you

n: A few months later Ishmael, a member of the royal family, murders Gedaliah and those with him—destroying the last hope of stable life in Judah.

f.g: Of the royal family; Ishmael may have resented a non-royal governor.

n: Fearing Babylonian revenge, the remaining people flee to Egypt—ironically returning to the land of bondage. They forced Jeremiah to go with them.
The book closes with a glimmer of hope. In 561 BC, after 37 years in captivity, Jehoiachin is released from prison by Babylon’s new king.

f.g: Amel-Marduk, son of Nebuchadnezzar; the name means “man of Marduk,” not “evil.”
An idiom for showing favor or releasing someone (compare Genesis 40:13).

n: The Babylonian king treats Jehoiachin kindly and honors him above other captive kings.

f.w: set his throne above the throne of the kings

n: Jehoiachin trades prison clothes for royal ones and eats regularly at the king’s table. Babylonian ration tablets even mention food given to “Jehoiachin, king of Judah.”

f.g: A symbol of restored dignity.

n: He receives a daily allowance for life. Ending here, the book quietly signals that David’s line survives and God’s promises are not finished; Jehoiachin’s descendants include Zerubbabel and, in Matthew’s genealogy, Jesus.

f.w: all the days of his life
